newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Wall Str factor, but economy key for C.Euro shares.
newsitem.headline: Wall Str factor, but economy key for C.Euro shares.

text.p: Warsaw and Budapest lost ground after Wall Street's two-day fall but analysts said local economic conditions, more than New York trends, set the tone of the market.

"There isn't a logical reason why Wall Street and central Europe should be correlated at all," said James Oates, director for Central and East Europe at UBS in London. "The interest rate cycle, the earning cycle is completely different."
Some analysts said big falls in the U.S. could lead to the same in Budapest and Warsaw but others were unconvinced of a strong link with the Dow.

"U.S. investors are not going to take money from emerging markets because the latter offer a very high return and a very high risk," said Mateusz Andrzejewski, analyst at Bank Pekao SA brokerage, referring to the recent U.S. Funds rate rise.

"There is nothing to do against a fall of four percent in Wall Street in two days but a half percent move in either direction hasn't any direct impact on the Hungarian market," said Gyorgy Czipo, trader at ING Barings in Budapest.
Nevertheless, analysts largely agree the Hungarian share market is perhaps the most exposed to changes on Wall Street among the central European markets.
"My feeling is that Hungary might be a little bit more correlated simply because there are a lot more overseas investors in the Hungarian market as a proportion," Oates said.
Wall Street's dip last Thursday and this Monday had a varied impact on the central European markets, partly due to divergencies in opening times around Easter.
The Budapest bourse, surviving last Friday with a dip of 25.27 points, surrendered on Tuesday giving up 1.78 percent before a 0.64 percent recovery to 5,353.49 points on Wednesday.

In Warsaw on Wednesday the main WIG-index tumbled another 3.1 percent to 15,596.2 points in addition to Tuesday's 3.5 percent loss. Analysts said that after a rebound seen on Thursday investors would remain focused on foreign bourses.

In Moscow, Wall Street had drawn investor attention away from Russian shares, traders said, and the market's daily turnover had fallen to near $20 million, half what traders now consider healthy levels.

Operators in Russia gave mixed predictions for the rest of the week though prices of some leading shares firmed on Wednesday and the RTS-23 share index hovered near 300 all day after declining early in the week.
"We have to wait for the Dow Jones," said Pavel Gronbjerg, head of equities trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow.
Prague and Bratislava were hardly affected, with the Czech PX50 index losing some half percent on Wednesday, after remaining virtually unchanged on Tuesday and last Friday.

The Bucharest bourse, which performed poorly for most of 1996, has shown signs of revival this year as domestic institutional investors returned to the market and foreigners started taking an interest in Romanian equities.

Romanian traders said positive signs from the new centrist government heralding a stabilisation of the leu currency and encouragement for portfolio investors are likely to draw in more investors, boosting volumes and prices.
On the Slovenian market valuation triggered investors for new purchases which pushed the SBI index up 1.73 percent to 1,303.68 points on Wednesday, raising the week's gains to 2.3 percent.

"Obviously investors regarded prices as low enough to start buying, if similar demand continues until the end of the week, then maybe we can say our market has finally picked up," Jerney Obed, trader at A bank, said.

The Croatian market, although exposed to international factors, had all eyes on the local elections on April 13, hoping it will bring a revival from the current sluggish trend. -- Budapest newsroom +36 1 327-4040
